A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers
I drift off into a world of my own
make sure never to be alone with another person

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
I feel like an object, not like a person
You can never know who will harm you

Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items
issues.explanation: The profile contains several items implying an active sense of present threat or exposure (e.g., 'World is Dangerous', 'Exposed to Others', concealment to avoid being noticed), yet the Threat component is entirely absent. For this trauma type, such items would usually cohere with at least some explicit threat content; the omission makes the cross-node picture clinically uneven.

'World is Dangerous' expresses a broad ongoing threat belief, but the formulation specifies no active links into or out of Threat and no Threat items are endorsed. This makes the appraisal sit awkwardly in the formulation because it functions more like a threat belief than an isolated negative self-appraisal.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
issues.explanation: 'Concealing Clothing ... to avoid being noticed' implies active management of current interpersonal threat/visibility. With Threat completely unrepresented and no Trigger→Threat or Maladaptive Strategies→Threat linkage in the formulation, this strategy lacks a clear matching symptom target in the rest of the profile.

Threat: missing/none selected despite multiple current-danger and exposure-related items

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: The Threat node is not clinically coherent here. 'Flashbacks' and 'Physical Reactivity' are re-experiencing/arousal responses rather than threat appraisals, while the only genuine threat appraisal selected is 'Threat from Strangers.' That mixes different constructs within one node.

vignette:
The man who came to therapy, who asked to be called Marcus, was twenty-five years old and worked as a housekeeper for a small hotel chain. He was single and lived alone in a studio apartment he kept meticulously clean. He had been referred by his primary care doctor after a series of panic-like episodes at work, but when he sat down in the chair, he did not immediately speak about the hotel. He spoke about the dark.

Marcus's trauma was not a single event but a texture of years. Between the ages of six and twelve, he had been physically abused by his mother's boyfriend, a man named Dale. Dale worked nights and slept during the day, and the abuse happened in the hours after Marcus was supposed to be asleep. Dale would come into his room, pull him out of bed by the arm, and strike him with whatever was at hand-a belt, a wooden spoon, the flat of his hand. The worst times were when Dale forced him to kneel on the bare floor in the corner of the living room, facing the wall, for hours at a time. Marcus learned to stay perfectly still, to make himself as small and silent as possible, because any sound-a sniffle, a shift of weight-would bring another blow. What he remembered most vividly, what came back to him now with full sensory force, was the feel of the cheap linoleum under his knees: a slightly sticky, cool, diamond-patterned surface that his skin would imprint with sweat. The memory would hit him without warning-the cold floor, the smell of Dale's cigarette smoke, the sound of the television muttering in the next room, the dim light from a streetlamp through the blinds-and he would be there again, completely, his heart slamming, his breath gone, his body frozen in a position of surrender.

As an adult, Marcus had built a life around never being caught off guard. He had learned that you could never know who would harm you, and that the people who seemed safest were often the most dangerous. He had also come to believe that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him. He felt exposed, as though his history were written on his skin, and he dreaded the moment someone would look at him and know. This feeling was strongest when he was alone with another person. He had developed a quiet rule: never be alone with anyone, not even for a moment. At work, he timed his cleaning of guest rooms to avoid intersecting with guests in the hallways. He would wait in the supply closet until he heard a door close and footsteps fade, and only then emerge. His coworkers thought he was shy or odd, but they left him alone. He had also begun to drop responsibilities that required him to be around others. He had stopped visiting his sister because she lived with a roommate, and he could not bear the idea of being in an apartment with two people he did not fully trust. He had stopped going to the grocery store at normal hours, instead shopping at three in the morning when the aisles were empty.

The most powerful escape Marcus had was in his own mind. When the world became too threatening-when a child cried in the hotel lobby, when the cleaning cart's wheel made a sound like a footstep, when his hand brushed against a stiff polyester sheet that felt like linoleum-he would drift off into a world of his own. He would imagine himself somewhere else entirely: a quiet beach, a forest, a room with no doors. In these fantasies, he was safe. But the problem was that the fantasies were becoming harder to reach. The real world kept breaking through. The memories were not just thoughts; they were full sensory relivings that overwhelmed him so completely he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes for minutes at a time. His body reacted before his mind could catch up-sweating, shaking, his stomach clenching as if he were about to be hit. At night, he dreaded waking up in the dark, because the dark was when Dale had come. He would lie rigid in bed, listening, his whole body primed for a blow that no longer came.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a specific incident at the hotel. A guest had left a child unattended in a room, and the child had begun to cry-a high, thin, desperate wail that cut through the hallway. Marcus was standing outside with his cart, and the sound hit him like a physical force. He dropped the cleaning spray and walked away. He walked out of the hotel, down the street, and kept walking until he found himself in a park, sitting on a bench, shaking. He did not go back to work that day. He did not call his supervisor. He simply disappeared. When he finally went home, he realized he could not keep doing this. He was afraid of what he might lose next-his job, his apartment, his tenuous grip on a life that already felt borrowed. He came to therapy because he was exhausted, and because he was beginning to wonder if there was a world in which he did not have to be on guard every second. He was not sure such a world existed, but he was willing to ask.
